cards.b: Decomposition of an ionic compound, when molten or in aqueous solution, by passing an electric current.
Anode = positive electrode; cathode = negative electrode.
The molten or aqueous substance that is decomposed by electrolysis.

cards.f: Why must ionic solids be molten or dissolved?
cards.b: Ions must be free to move to the electrodes; in a solid lattice they are fixed.
Platinum or graphite/carbon; they do not react or take part.
Cathode: metals or hydrogen. Anode: non-metals (other than hydrogen), e.g. chlorine, bromine, oxygen.
Cathode: hydrogen; anode: chlorine; NaOH(aq) left in solution.
Cathode: hydrogen; anode: oxygen (volume ratio H₂ : O₂ = 2 : 1).
Cathode: copper deposited (brown); anode: oxygen. Blue colour fades.
Cathode gains copper; anode dissolves (loses mass). Blue colour stays the same.
Electrons move in the wire from anode to cathode; ions move in the electrolyte; cations to cathode, anions to anode.

cards.f: Hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell: product and advantage
cards.b: Only product is water, so no pollution at use; hydrogen and oxygen react to produce electricity.

cards.f: Fuel cell disadvantages vs petrol engine
cards.b: Hydrogen is difficult to store and make (often from fossil fuels); fewer refuelling stations; high cost.

gaps.s: In electrolysis the positive electrode is called the ___ .
Negative ions move towards the ___ during electrolysis.
During electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide, lead forms at the ___ .
The gas formed at the anode in concentrated sodium chloride solution is ___ .
The only chemical product of a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell is ___ .
Reduction at the cathode involves the ___ of electrons.

short.q: State the products at each electrode when molten lead(II) bromide is electrolysed, and give one observation. [3]
short.model: Cathode: lead; anode: bromine. Red-brown fumes seen at the anode.
points: red-brown fumes / silvery bead of lead

short.q: Why does solid sodium chloride not conduct but aqueous sodium chloride does? [2]
short.model: In the solid the ions cannot move. In solution they are free to move and carry charge.

short.q: Describe the changes seen when copper(II) sulfate solution is electrolysed with carbon electrodes. [3]
short.model: Brown copper deposits on the cathode, bubbles of oxygen form at the anode, and the blue colour of the solution fades.

short.q: Write the half-equation for the formation of sodium at the cathode and say whether it is oxidation or reduction. [2]
short.model: Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na; reduction (gain of electrons).

short.q: State two advantages of hydrogen–oxygen fuel cells compared with petrol engines. [2]
short.model: The only product is water so there are no pollutant gases (no CO₂, CO or NOx at the point of use); they are also more efficient.
points: only water/no carbon dioxide or toxic products
